papers.title: Near-Horizon Scalar-Wave Sampling: Rindler Bounds and Schwarzschild Comparison
papers.abstract: We study classical reconstruction of an outgoing scalar-wave component from radial-shell observations. Starting from the noncompact-time Rindler metric, we construct Klein--Gordon evolution by closed quadratic forms and reduce the massless characteristic dynamics to translation in optical distance. For an initial optical interval of length $L$, a shell of width $d$, and recording time $T$, the optimal squared observability bounds are $A(T,L)=\min\{d,(T-L)_+\}$ and $B(T,L)=\min\{d,T\}$. At $T=L$, the Rindler observation map is injective with nonclosed range. Discrete shell observations form a spatial fusion frame precisely when their transported regions cover the initial interval; we compute optimal uniform-grid bounds and characterize robustness under profile erasures. Finite-resolution reconstruction separates localization error, approximation error and noise amplification. For fixed Schwarzschild mass and angular momentum, we compare the scalar-wave observation operator with its Rindler limit. Anchored finite-energy preparation permits arbitrary prescribed outgoing $L^2([-L,0])$ profiles without a zero-integral condition. The operator error is explicitly $O(e^{-2\kappa a})$ as an apparatus of fixed optical size is translated toward the horizon; whenever $T>L$, positive Rindler bounds transfer to Schwarzschild for all sufficiently large $a$. A positive Schwarzschild lower bound is impossible at or below the optical travel time, for every translation. These results concern classical observation and reconstruction, not quantum information or dissipative horizon evolution.

papers.title: OFFER (One-Formula-Facilitates-Every-Relation) for Calculus
papers.abstract: The large number of calculus formulas makes learning calculus heavily memory-dependent and can scare away many students. Based on Issac Newton's idea of prediction, this paper shows that calculus students need to master only one critical formula: his proposition that, given boundary data, one can predict the interior and vice versa. We can treat other formulas as consequences of the formula for this proposition. In 1-, 2-, and 3-dimensional spaces, this formula corresponds to the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem, and the divergence theorem. This approach is summarized as OFFER (one-formula-facilitates-every-relationship) for calculus education. This paper demonstrates the method and advantages of the OFFER pedagogy. The OFFER approach can accelerate the pace of calculus teaching, provide deeper insight into calculus, inspire questions from students, and naturally facilitate the inclusion of real-world data, artificial intelligence (AI), and computer coding in the calculus series. Consequently, OFFER may serve as a way to modernize calculus curricula in the era of AI and the digital economy.

papers.title: Approximating the Ellipse Perimeter by "Bending the Line": The ELIP Closed-Form Family
papers.abstract: The perimeter of an ellipse is expressed exactly through the complete elliptic integral of the second kind, motivating accurate closed-form approximations. We introduce ELIP (Ellipse Linear Interpolated Perimeter), a family built by correcting the straight line joining the two exact normalized endpoint values. Two branches are developed: logarithmic-power corrections with optional deformation and exponential modulators, and rational-logarithmic corrections incorporating the exact asymptotic behavior of highly elongated ellipses. The framework distinguishes coefficients fixed analytically by Maclaurin matching from parameters optimized numerically by minimax fitting. Compact rationalized formulas achieve maximum relative errors of approximately 6.84, 3.57, 0.904, and 1.596 ppm. An ELIP R5,2 + 3 log formula with three fitted degrees of freedom has a certified maximum relative error below 0.001623 ppm. For ELIP R5,3 + 3 log, all rational-core coefficients are determined by exact Maclaurin matching. A one-parameter multiplicative correction, 1 - A*h^12*(1-h)^(7/4), reduces the certified global error bound to below 0.000452 ppm. This formula matches the exact perimeter series through h^8, while the correction starts at order h^12. The results provide a systematic approach combining exact endpoint geometry, local series constraints, elongated-limit logarithmic asymptotics, and low-dimensional numerical optimization.

papers.title: A Local Proof of Langlands's First Main Lemma for Local Epsilon Factors over Nonarchimedean Local Fields
papers.abstract: We give a complete local proof of Langlands's First Main Lemma for local epsilonfactors over nonarchimedean local fields. The proof builds on Dwork's p-adic calculations and Langlands's formulation of the local method. The present paper reformulates these calculations in a common normalization and extends the argument to equal characteristic. A more systematic treatment of stationary parameters and conductor cases is intended to make the calculations easier to follow. The author has also completed a local proof of Langlands's Second Main Lemma. Together with the present result and Langlands's remaining reductions, this gives a complete proof of the local construction of local epsilon factors envisioned by Langlands.
